en: Verses of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Exposition of the Holy Teachings),
composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by imperial decree.

The Sugata has excellently taught the sublime three bodies; To the fearless, untainted realization and the Dharma he taught, And to the sons of the Muni who uphold the truth of the Supreme Vehicle— I now offer praise and prostration with the utmost sincerity.
I prostrate and pay homage with reverence to the Great Compassionate One, who is about to succeed to the rank of the Dharma King of All-Knowledge,
the refuge for the world that has no other support, and the one who proclaims the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
In the past, I, Asaṅga, heard this from him; now I shall interweave the essentials of the stages (bhūmi).
Out of compassion for the holy teaching, I shall manifest it with concise phrasing, comprehensive meaning, and ease of understanding.
The skillful mastery in the meaning of the pure *saṃgrahavastu*, the contemplation (*abhisamaya*) of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness,
and the inconceivable yoga— these are the eleven chapters on the supreme discernment of the *saṃgraha*.
All realms, afflictions, The truths, the bases, the factors of enlightenment,
The person, the fruits, and all virtues— these are the nine topics.
Mind, mental factors, form, Dissociated phenomena, and the unconditioned.
The realms refer to the desire realm, the form realm, and so forth, as well as the three-thousandfold world system.
One should know that the nature of afflictions, karma, and birth constitutes the defilements;
the truths are of six kinds.
Based on the eight and the two, the factors of enlightenment are manifold; first, there are thirty-seven.
Then there are knowledge and the doors of liberation, the tracks of practice, and serenity and insight.
The dwelling place and its basis, the generation of the mind and compassion,
the various practices and the nature of penetration, the stages, and the perfections.
The bodhisattva practices and the means of attraction, as well as those gates of dhāraṇīs and samādhis,
the various immeasurable mental engagements, the characteristics of mental engagement with suchness,
and the inconceivable resolute belief— these are [the topics].
One should know the various enumerations of the vast *āśaya*:
the seven beginning with those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), as well as the eight types to be known;
furthermore, those such as the "seven-times-at-most" (*saptakṛdbhavaparama*), and the six types beginning with those of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*).
The seven types beginning with those of dull faculties, those who are householders and those who have left home,
the three vehicles such as the Śrāvaka-yāna, those who are savable and those who are unsavable;
the nine beginning with those who enter skillful means, and the two due to differences in birth.
Furthermore, due to the distinctions among the realms, one should know there are thirteen types.
There are five kinds of abandonment of results; there are thorough knowledges and purifications.
Purity, result, realm, and enlightenment—these are the unlearned [qualities] according to their own enumeration.
Abandonment occurs through the severance of many causes;
the basis from which abandonment proceeds is established by means of attention, reliance, cultivation, and the attainment of the successive stages of abandonment.
One should understand the distinctions of abandonment, as well as the characteristics and benefits of abandonment;
thus, according to what has been taught, one should further understand its many varieties.
The immeasurables, the various liberations, the spheres of mastery, and the spheres of totality—
The absence of strife, the knowledge of wondrous vows, the analytical knowledges, and the supernormal powers;
the marks and minor signs, their purity, as well as the powers, the fearlessnesses, the ways of non-protection,
the foundations of mindfulness, and the eternal severance of all habitual tendencies.
The sublime Dharma that is never forgotten, the great compassion of the Tathāgata,
the qualities unique to a Buddha, and the sublime wisdom of all modes—
know that these nine preceding matters serve as the basis for the first two.
The next two and the final six categories subsume the defiled and the purified:
because they are the distinctions of the basis of defilement, because they are the objects of purification,
because the mind does not disperse, and because they are the skillful means of correct cultivation.
Because of the distinctions in those stages, because of the causes such as verbal expression,
because of their results, and because of their qualities, the number and sequence are exactly thus.
One who wishes to contemplate the immeasurable varieties of questions and answers [should know this].
Through the speech of the Buddhas, because of the inclusion of phenomena and their characteristics:
phrases, delusion, and conceptual proliferation; abiding, reality, purity, and excellence;
tranquility, nature, and principle; provisional designation, and clear realization.
Location, position, and differentiation; Activity, maintenance, increase, and decrease;
darkness, speech, what is perceived, and the superior; Detachment, transformation, and concealment-protection.
Discernment and manifestation, sleep and association,
the various inclusions and conjunctions, exposition, support, and sequence.
Activity, object, and yoga; śamatha and vipaśyanā;
the various forms of attention and instruction; qualities, awakening, and the holy teaching.
If one wishes to practice correctly for the sake of attaining qualities such as omniscience,
one should rely upon ten types of dharma-practice and six modes of reasoning.
This is the most excellent among all treatises and provides skillful entry into yoga.
The meaning of purity should be understood as being endowed with four qualities of purity:
because it encompasses all meanings;
because it is indestructible by external factors; [and so forth].
Because it is easy to enter;
and having entered, because one’s practice is not lost or destroyed.
The Buddhas preach the sublime Dharma, correctly relying upon the two truths:
The first is called the conventional; the second is called the ultimate.
The initial teaching of self, phenomena, and their functions is spoken for the sake of conforming to others.
The sevenfold and the fourfold suchness are named the ultimate.
One should understand the distinctions of intrinsic nature, meaning, establishment, number, sequence, and skillfulness;
these clarify the conventional meaning of the aggregates.
The five, the three dharmas, and reality; furthermore, those four should be known, as well as the four kinds of thorough investigation and the four kinds of knowledge of things as they truly are.
The establishment of the three natures, their differentiation, their activity, and their concealment—
Skillful means, inclusion, and distinctions— each of these has many varieties.
Having heard the twelvefold teaching, the three supreme refuges, the three trainings,
and the three types of enlightenment, they are taught for the purification of sentient beings.
Hearing, taking refuge, training, and awakening—six, three, twelve, and five;
according to the sequence of their names and numbers, they shall be analyzed extensively as appropriate.
The noble conduct, the supreme vehicle, great enlightenment, and its qualities;
the heterodox views, the methods of debate, and their refutations—each of these should be known to have many varieties.
Extraordinary and non-extraordinary, equanimity of mind and benefiting others,
repaying kindness and joyful praise, and the practice of non-empty skillful means.
Through non-erroneous skillful means, they cause beings to fall back or to advance;
through both semblance and actual virtues, they skillfully discipline sentient beings.
All bodhisattvas receive their prediction and enter the stage of certainty.
That which is definitively performed and that which should always be performed— this should be known as the most excellent Dharma.
The establishment of all designations, the investigation of all phenomena,
as well as thorough knowledge according to reality, together with all the immeasurables.
The proclamation of the benefits of the fruit, the nature and inclusion of the Mahāyāna, and the ten things a bodhisattva should know; the establishment of various names and designations;
the adherence to the view that the effect exists within the cause, the theory of manifestation, and the existence of the past and future.
Self, permanence, the cause of past actions, Īśvara and so forth, the harmful dharma,
the finite and infinite, evasive speech, the view of no-cause, annihilationism, emptiness,
regarding [wrong views] as supreme, pure, and auspicious— these are called the sixteen heterodox doctrines.
Function has no intrinsic nature; to claim it both includes and excludes [its object] is contradictory.
To assert that it is either functional or non-functional as a cause results in great fallacies.
One should discuss its essence, its locus, its evidence, and its adornment.
The defeat in debate, the departure from debate, and the many duties;
the nature of the method of explaining the meaning of the text; the raising of objections regarding the meaning and the sequence of the teacher;
the assembly listening and praising the Buddha; and the benefits of learning in brief and in detail.

One should understand the meaning of the brief and extensive [explanations] regarding the mental engagement with the characteristics of the stages, their bases, virtues and non-virtues, the objects to be countered and their antidotes.
Regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, as well as the various laws of dependent origination—
One should know the skillful means regarding the possible and the impossible, the faculties, and the truths.
Regarding the body, there is mastery and so forth; the body exists without a cause, it undergoes transmigration, performs various karmas, and possesses two kinds of predominance.
Regarding the body, there is the sense of origination; Regarding reality, the sense of being sustained by a self;
Regarding transmigration, the sense of an agent; And the sense of various forms of sovereignty.
Whether in defilement or purification, Seven kinds of delusion arise.
To counteract this, one should know that it is subsumed within the seven types of skillfulness.
Those who falsely imagine a self in the body rely upon the sense faculties for their abiding;
they revolve amidst sensory objects and experience what is pleasant and unpleasant.
The basis for verbal expression, the agent, and the conscious subject—
by means of these distinct aggregates, one perceives them as a single body.
Because of this initial cause of delusion, one conceives of a permanent cause or no cause at all.
I abide as the master of the sense faculties, capable of contact and capable of sensation.
From this place of death and birth, there is that which is reckoned as the transmigrator;
it is the agent of dharma and non-dharma, as well as the sovereign over its results.
Regarding the practice of wrong conduct, they conceive it as defilement;
regarding the practice of right conduct, they falsely conceive it as liberation.
Before the Buddha appeared in the world, such delusion prevailed.
Because the Buddha has appeared in the world, he has taught the seven kinds of skillfulness.
Through knowing the distinctions such as the world and so forth, one can eliminate the notion of a unified whole;
thus, there is detachment and liberation, for sentient beings cannot be apprehended.

One should know the skillfulness regarding the aggregates (skandha-kauśalya) through the wisdom that discerns the various, the summarized, the commonalities, the distinctions, the increases, and the decreases.
Because one sees that [the aggregates] arise from three causes, it is called skillfulness regarding the elements (dhātu-kauśalya).
From beginningless time, from its own seeds, various things arise in manifold ways;
through this and by means of this, no grasper can be found.
Because it is established by means of one's own wisdom, it is able to eliminate inferiority.
Knowing that all contacts and all sensations arise through two kinds of gateways,
and that they depend upon contact, one should know this as skill in the bases (*āyatana-kauśalya*).
Knowing the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and the divine spheres (*devāyatana*), which serve as the successive supports, [one attains mastery].
By means of conventional truth, one understands the two natures.
Knowing that the unceased is impermanent, and that causes are able to produce various effects,
with their own continuities being similar— this is called skill in dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*).
Sentient beings cannot be apprehended, yet there is one who abandons and continues [existence], because they have thoroughly realized the fourfold dependent origination that is profoundly deep.
There is no acting, no proceeding, and no attainment; nor do two or other entities undergo transformation.
Pure vision is free from residual karma; it is neither "self" nor "sovereignty.
Such wisdom knows the skillful means regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*):
that which is fixed within its own fruit is called "possible," while that which differs from this is called "impossible."

Regarding the arising and abiding of the grasper, as well as defilement and purification, there is no rational basis for observing a self other than these; yet it exercises sovereignty over their results.
Skillfulness regarding such means is called "expertise in the faculties" (indriya-kauśalya).
That is to say, because they exercise sovereignty over the arising, abiding, defilement, and purification of grasping;
because of the two natures of suffering; because [the alternatives] are logically untenable due to conjunction;
and because of the absence of cause, the presence of cause, and the five types of analogies.
Because one awakens to it in this way, one should know the skillfulness regarding the truths.
One awakens to what was never seen before, and to the causes and conditions for meanings not yet received.
One should know that these various skillful means are distinguished by twenty-three types.
Preceded by the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, it is subsequently most perfectly pure.
Impermanence refers to the conditioned, because it is associated with the three characteristics;
the meaning of impermanence should be understood accordingly in six and eight ways.
Non-existence, destruction, transformation, separation, acquisition, and future existence;
The momentary, the continuous, and the like—due to the mind, the vessel, and the objects of enjoyment.
One should know that transformation has fifteen distinct varieties, namely those of the states (*avasthā*) and so forth, due to being impelled by eight conditions.
In the lower realm (*adhodhātu*), all are present; in the middle realm (*madhyadhātu*), three gates are absent.
Possessing three kinds of transformation, with the receptacle world further excluded from the upper realms;
the meaning of impermanence as the absence of intrinsic nature is that which is grasped through the parikalpita (imagined) nature.
The remaining meanings of impermanence should be understood as pertaining to the paratantra (dependent) nature.
All that is impermanent is suffering, for it is intermingled with manifold sufferings;
the deluded fool, ignorant of the nature of phenomena, does not perceive the harm he incurs.
Because it is the fruit of that mind, once arisen, it naturally perishes.
The subsequent occurrence of transformation should be understood as momentary cessation.
Through the predominance of mental perfuming, there is mastery over meditative transformation;
this is the principle of the arising of images, as well as the three types of scriptural authority.
Because it contradicts the cause of arising, there are no causes for abiding or cessation;
otherwise, there would be the faults of spontaneous abiding and permanence.
One should know that it ceases spontaneously, not through water, fire, or wind, because [these elements] arise and cease simultaneously with it.
Once that [cause] has ceased along with its concomitants, it is the cause for the arising of other transformations.
When the continuity of the contradictory is severed, the two characteristics become non-characteristic;
this contradicts what is perceived by the world, as there would be neither a phenomenon nor any other cause.
It is not that the body, milk, forests, and so forth, were previously without change,
nor is it that they do not perish initially, only to be extinguished at the very last moment.
This is because the various states, thoughts, and afflictions are characterized by impermanence and transformation.
If this were without transformation, then experience, action, and liberation would be irrational.
Because functional capacity would not exist, there would be the contradiction of being both included and not included;
thus, the reasons [proffered] for its having utility or lacking utility would result in logical fallacies.
The characteristics of transformation of intrinsic nature—whether as existent or non-existent—are illogical;
there would be no distinction [between states], and impermanence would entail five faults if there were distinction.
There would be no characteristic and no cause, nor would intrinsic nature be eternally different.
If there were no prior change, I would be eternally liberated.
It is illogical for that which is eternal to be created, due to two or three reasons;
because of their predominance over objects and sentient beings, atoms are not eternal.
Impermanence is their basis, evolving through successive distinctions;
because sensations and so forth differ, one should know that consciousness is impermanent.
Lack of knowledge regarding impermanence is the root of the four perversions.
One should know that in this world, the power of delusion increases further.
Through heedlessness, indolence, [wrong] views, ignorance, lack of provisions,
evil friends, and non-Dharma— know these to be the causes of lack of wisdom.
Improper mental attention, recollecting the past and so forth, proceeds as a continuous succession of similar states; one conceives the impermanent to be permanent.
Arising at the beginning, end, and middle, one grasps the three characteristics of conditioned phenomena.
The wisdom that tames impermanence should be known to arise from two causes.
That vision is of six kinds, as well as four kinds regarding dependent origination.
Because it arises from its own seeds, it does not come from another; because it depends on conditions, it is not self-originated.
Because it is unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*), it is not common; because it functions, it is not without cause.
Arising is for the sake of abandoning causes, and cessation is the desire for the harmony of arising.
Through the inversion of non-inversion, there is weary detachment; that cause is the characteristic of suffering.
Based on the distinctions of the three feelings, the three characteristics of suffering are established;
therefore, it is said that all feelings are, in their essential nature, suffering.
One should know that the nature of conditioned phenomena is suffering because they are all accompanied by coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Attachment and equanimity are illogical, as they share the fault of lacking liberation.
There are obstacles such as gain and deep [afflictions]; by relying on diligence and abiding in the vehicle of emptiness, one abandons attachment, inferior nature, inversion, and defilement.
Like an abscess, scabies, or leprosy, it is the basis for the three types of sensation;
it gives rise to the three kinds of contact, which proceed in accordance with the grasping of pleasure and so forth.
Its specific characteristic, its own conceptualization, and its nature of non-quiescence constitute suffering.
Fifty-five [factors] should be known as being subsumed within the three types of suffering.
Due to differences in realm, object-condition, body, destiny, species, truth, the three periods of time,
temporal duration, life-force, and category, they bring about the various distinctions among manifold sufferings.
One should know that there are three types of stages for those who have not yet abandoned desire for form and so forth:
all varieties exist in the desire realm, while in the form and formless realms, two are excluded.
The conventional has two types; the ultimate is said to be the universal.
The two [types of] objects extend to the higher stages; one should know that there is no manifest defilement therein.
It is not that the burden of the formless realm is absent; rather, it consists of the pervasive heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the gods and the final limit of the truths.
The remaining seven are the secondary fetters (*anuvyañjana-bandhana*) of the higher realms.
One should know that birth and the other [links of dependent origination] each have fivefold distinctions;
they are associated with the heaviness of suffering (*duḥkha-dauṣṭhulya*) and serve as the basis for the three types of suffering.
The final [link] and the penultimate [link] each serve as the basis for four types of suffering.
That is to say: birth, the root of birth, as well as the nature of suffering and transformation.
Included within the three time periods, the two conditions of suffering are not the highest;
it should be known that all other sufferings mentioned belong to the desire realm.
Through loss of mindfulness and lack of effort, through distraction and improper reflection,
through incorrect comprehension and delusion, and by means of heedlessness and the like;
because of dullness, because of weakness, and because of the arousal of heedlessness.
Because the continuity is severed, one should know that forgetfulness arises.
Due to dullness, due to negligence, due to cherishing the present life,
and due to lack of faith in future suffering, there is the initiation [of action] without effort.
Because they evolve as a similar continuity, due to the habitual practice of grasping at objects as a whole in opposition to false conceptualization, the four kinds of perversions arise.
These consist of distinctions of realm, distinctions of dependent origination, distinctions of stage, and distinctions of sequence.
And regarding the distinctions in their continuity, one should know that each has many varieties.

Through faith-understanding and analytical investigation, with an undistracted mind and weary detachment, there are the paths of seeing, cultivation, and the ultimate; furthermore, they are like the eleven [factors] mentioned previously.
The fetters, doubt, and lack of delight in renunciation; Sinking, the evil destinies, and other destinies— Arising from inferior conduct, these exhaust all pervasive and individual sufferings.
If that which is here does not exist, and whatever else exists apart from it,
then according to these two principles, the characteristic of emptiness is said to be non-dual.
One should know this profound correspondence, wherein there is neither grasping nor abandoning, and no increase or decrease.
The distinctions are manifold, as they have been taught in various ways.
Because it would entail the fault of being merely conventional, because it would entail the fault that the aggregates lack a self,
and because it would entail the fault that the self lacks a body, the three types of self are untenable.
Like a master, fire, light, or space, it would have the faults of being distinct from its basis and dependent upon others;
it would be impermanent, devoid of functional activity, neither a cause nor a self.
I alone must be merely conventional; no analogy can be found for me.
The seven analogies are false conceptualizations, as are the three [cases] beginning with "one who sees.
If, like a seed, I were impermanent, then the agent would necessarily be conventional.
Just as one who has accomplished supernormal powers should exercise mastery over the mundane world,
so too am I like the earth and like space; I should be subject to impermanence and lack of intrinsic nature,
and should be like those two [earth and space] in being unconditioned, yet karma can still be clearly perceived.
That which can burn and that which can sever are functions performed solely by fire and the like;
the self, with respect to its possession of vision and so forth, is not like a knife or fire.
Just as the function of illumination is inseparable from light and has no distinct entity apart from it, [so too is the self].
Therefore, regarding both the internal and external, the principle of emptiness and selflessness is established.
Just as external worldly objects undergo benefit or harm apart from a self,
so too, although there is no real self within, the principles of defilement and purity are nonetheless established.
Because the states, volitions, and afflictions are impermanent and subject to change,
if the self were eternal and unchanging, then experiencing, acting, and liberation would be impossible.
The nature of phenomena arises from conditions, manifesting in a continuous succession;
having causes yet remaining unstable, it is called "transformation" due to its variation.
Like the body, a sprout, a river, or a lamp, it possesses various functions.
The self is eternally unchanging; it is illogical for it to undergo transformation or return [to its original state].
To give rise to names and concepts based on a self leads to two kinds of faults;
therefore, throughout all things, a real nature of self is entirely non-existent.
For the sake of ease of expression, for conformity with the world, for the severing of fear, and for the manifestation of both gain and loss.
A sudden awakening to disorder arises; it is perceptible in the world.
Action preceded by consciousness has ten kinds of faults.
Consciousness, self, cause, effort, and Īśvara— each having two [faults],
along with having a cause and being without a cause— one should know these ten kinds of faults.
One should know that there are five types of metaphors: non-determination, pervasive, augmentation, the baseless, and the false view of fear regarding objects.
These consist of non-substantiality and detachment, which are eliminated by relying on three kinds [of wisdom].
The antidotes to the various perceptions of bondage are of sixteen distinct types:
intrinsic nature and attachment, lack of comprehension, loss of mindfulness,
the universal, the partial, and the flow of the distinctions of delusion.
Abiding in the Dharma, seeking one's own mind, abiding in one's own mind, removing fetters and fears,
non-duality, defilement and purity— thus one realizes the principle of true emptiness.
The distinctions of cultivation are eighteenfold; some are with poison and some are without.
One should know that there are briefly two types for counteracting the five kinds of grasping.
The fruits of cultivation should be known as the merits of the three forms of awakening.
Based on the nature of the transformation of the support, the tasks to be accomplished are fulfilled.
One should know the three natures: first, the thoroughly imagined;
second, the dependent origination; and finally, the perfected reality.
The three kinds of naturelessness should be known as not being separate from the three natures:
by way of the naturelessness of characteristics, the naturelessness of arising, and ultimate naturelessness.
They are not subsumed within the five categories; beyond these, nothing else exists.
Because names function toward objects, the two are mutually adventitious.
Since no cognition occurs prior to the name, and because there are multiple names and lack of definiteness,
it is established that the functioning [of names] toward both existent and non-existent objects is irrational.
Because one grasps [an object] and establishes a name for it, others are unable to grasp it in that same way;
like the false attachments of sentient beings, this superimposition constitutes perversion (*viparyāsa*).
Through habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*), the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) arises, and based upon this, perversion is produced.
Thus, acting as mutual conditions for one another, they arise in succession.

Regarding intrinsic nature and its distinctions, there are: awakening, latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), application (*prayoga*), and pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*); furthermore, these should be known as fivefold.
There are eight kinds of discrimination, which can give rise to three things;
one should know that the essence of discrimination consists of the mind and mental factors of the three realms.
Bound by two fetters, they stubbornly cling to the two natures.
Therefore, regarding the liberation from the two bonds, there is truly neither attainment nor vision.
If there were a basis or cause even conventionally, then the two kinds [of purity] would be destroyed;
since defilement can be found, one should know that this is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
The characteristics have the coarse and heavy (*dauṣṭhulya*) as their essence; these arise through mutual conditioning and do not exist by way of self-nature.
Therefore, it is said that arising is without intrinsic nature (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāva*).
It is neither definitively existent nor non-existent, and this is accepted in all its aspects.
Comprising both the nominal and the substantial natures, that which is conventionally described as existing—
the proclamation of the self and the functions of phenomena— is all termed the conventional truth.
One should know that the ultimate truth consists of the seven kinds of suchness.
The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is the object of the two supreme wisdoms;
it is free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and is remote from identity and difference.
It is the pure objective referent (*ālambana*), eternally without change.
The nature of goodness and the nature of bliss—both are fully accomplished.
In reality, the ultimate lacks intrinsic nature because the self of conceptual proliferation does not exist;
since the dependent lacks those characteristics, it too lacks intrinsic nature in the ultimate sense.
Based on the three characteristics, one should know that five kinds of characteristics are established;
according to their respective applications, each has its own five functions.
Due to the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), the deluded worldling gives rise to the grasping at a sentient being (*sattvagrāha*).
When one realizes the nature of phenomena, the grasping at a self in phenomena is severed.
Regarding the first [nature], the dependent, grasping arises; through habitual perfuming, it becomes defiled.
Regarding the perfected, which is free from grasping; through habitual perfuming, it becomes purified.
Defiled, it is of the nature of outflows; purified, it is without outflows.
One should know that this transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is of two kinds, inconceivable:
the true reality and the self-nature, as well as tranquility and its qualities.
All that is inconceivable should be known to arise from four paths.
There are two kinds of śrāvakas: those who seek tranquility and those who seek enlightenment;
by relying on the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya), they proceed toward unsurpassed perfect awakening.
The transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) of the śrāvakas is attained through the cultivation of aversion and turning away;
the bodhisattva’s cultivation through skillful means relies upon non-dual wisdom,
for they do not abide in arising and ceasing.
The wisdom of all Buddhas is unsurpassed, bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings; it is inconceivable and non-dual.
One should know that what is currently observed—whether phenomena of inferior, middling, or superior grade, whether with outflows or without outflows—is not yet fully seen or experienced.
Supramundane superior wisdom, which can eliminate what is to be abandoned through seeing, is attained through non-conceptualization and relies solely upon meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
It is not present in the states of extreme distress, nor in the miserable realms; it is not present in the states of extreme joy, nor in the two higher [formless] realms.
Dwelling among humans and devas of the desire realm, the Buddha appears in the world for direct realization.

For those who have not yet abandoned desire, those who have partially abandoned it, and those who have fully abandoned it—for these, he alone attains perfect enlightenment; he is the most supreme one born from my lineage.
The self is not the cause of cognition, nor does it grasp objects by itself;
the self does not perceive through direct intuition, for it is clung to as a self.
Objects are impermanent, and cognition arises in dependence upon conditions.
Because the three types of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) and so forth have been severed,
one relies on the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the mind. Once the mental continuum has reached maturity—
whether through hearing the true Dharma or by naturally engaging in extremely appropriate mental attention— one attains direct realization.
Fixing the mind upon the object of focus, Diligently cultivating tranquility and concentration,
Through the increasing power of wholesome roots, One realizes the factors of the noble path of awakening.
From this, one enters the path of vision, And untainted right view arises.
One should know that the realization of clear observation (*abhisamaya*) consists in the permanent severance of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Although there is defilement within the miserable realms (*apāya*), the afflictions arising from conceptualization are severed.
Regarding the objects—the Teacher and so forth—these are subsumed under the three types of arising according to their respective categories.
By means of prior mundane knowledge, one discerns the ultimate truths; regarding these truths,
there is no further application of effort, and the characteristic of definitive arising—
the characteristic of the harmony between wisdom and its object— is reached at the culmination of all that is to be known.
One should know that the clear realization of the truths consists in ten kinds of certainty:
the certainty that my nature is not within the three realms of existence; that there is no cessation and no duality;
and that there is non-conceptualization and fearlessness, which is the certainty within the severance of self.
Initiation, realization, outflow, and fulfillment—these four stages are sequential;
furthermore, one should know that the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*) and so forth constitute the subsequent eight.
Abiding without regret in one’s object of focus, seeing the sphere of experience as it truly is,
relying on the path without delusion, and severing conduct through pure distinction—
these should be known as the three purities: purity of virtue, purity of mind, and [purity of view].
The path that relies upon the objective sphere is explained as the purification of wisdom.
Knowing the causes and conditions of the body and so forth, one skillfully penetrates the three periods of time;
next, one understands the four types of suffering, and furthermore, the eight types of suffering should be known.
From this correct contemplation of the truths, the wisdom of the sixteen aspects arises;
it serves as the basis for each subsequent stage in order to remedy the four inversions.
From this, one proceeds with further cultivation, becoming entirely weary of and detached from the mind.
Through the thorough investigation of the truths, certainty, and the arising of ultimate awakening,
there follow three moments of mind— liberating wisdom free from further application—
which comprise one hundred and twelve [moments] and subsume the ten abandonments of the afflictions.
These are the factors of enlightenment, characterized by six kinds of purified wisdom;
because they act without conceptual discrimination, they are established according to their functions.
When a bodhisattva is in this stage, they first cultivate the power of superior causes.
Regarding the suffering of oneself and others, one gives rise to a mind of equanimity.
This is the intention of the Great Self; since no self-nature is to be found, know that this vast intention is non-dual in nature, free from discrimination between the two.
The sixteen lines above represent the pure mundane knowledge;
because it serves as the antidote to the elements and stages, the ultimate task is accomplished.
This differentiation of clear realization consists of either six or eighteen aspects.
The advantages of the marks are manifold, as explained extensively in the sūtras and śāstras.
The yoga of the Prajñāpāramitā consists in non-conceptual meditative attainment;
because it is free from all conceptualization in every respect, it is "all-in-all."
In every respect and in all their aspects, there are the three characteristics, the three wheels, namely:
name, characteristic, defilement, purity, and the two kinds that are neither;
regarding phenomena and the emptiness of phenomena, there are no two kinds of conceptual proliferation.
Non-conceptuality would be endless; beyond this, it is not reasonable.
If there were nothing at all to be apprehended, there would be neither wisdom nor liberation;
both would become apprehensions of the ineffable, which would be useless for conforming [to reality].
The nine matters are inconceivable because they rely upon five bases;
there are five kinds of causes, and gain and loss are each of three types.
That which should not be thought and that which is not recorded— one should know these arise from four causes.
It is not fixed as one, for its profound depth leads to the persistence of meaningless characteristics.
One should not contemplate whether the self exists or does not exist, because that would result in two faults;
since those same two faults apply to others as well, one should not contemplate [the self] as being either identical to or different from them.
Although these two do not depend on views, they should not be conceptualized because they are established [as such];
for if one does not conceptualize them in this way, they are followed by three faults.
As for the happy and miserable realms, the two agents are not fixed.
The past karmas of good and evil, their locations, and their activities are inconceivable.
Suchness is the untainted nature; it accomplishes purposeful benefits.
Because the Tathāgata, who is meditative concentration, is peerless and sovereign.
That which is proclaimed by the non-Buddhists leads to what is meaningless;
it is irrational, far removed from the four states, and indeterminate—thus it should not be contemplated.
To exert effort in what is not the proper place is to revile the Great Self.
Because one does not cultivate pure virtue, three faults arise.
To distance oneself from the inconceivable and contemplate what is conceivable is to possess eight kinds of merit;
therefore, one should contemplate in accordance with reality.
That which has been taught by all Buddhas, The Omniscient One and others do not contradict;
Because of the five causes and two causes, One should not engage in speculative thought regarding this.
Number, characteristics, distinctions, existence, location, Limit, and origination—
Perception, skillfulness, gathering, and so forth—these are the superior determinations of all matters.
The nature of mind is twofold: maturation and transformation;
the first is the ālayavijñāna, and it should be known that seeds are of two kinds.
Appropriation, the initial [moment of consciousness], clarity, seeds, karma, bodily sensation,
the mindless attainments, and death— these would all be irrational if [the ālayavijñāna] did not exist.
The object-condition and the associated [factors] act as mutual causes for one another;
consciousness and the rest flow together, undergoing both defilement and cessation.
By the power of the support and the objective sphere, the distinctions of the mind are established.
Furthermore, by means of seven modes of activity, the mind’s bondage should be understood as difficult to comprehend:
its objects are not under its control; it dwells in a basis that is evil;
and it is driven by the power of conditions. Thus should the bondage of the mind be known.
Distractedness and abiding, the sixfold and the fifteenfold;
the objects of the six [consciousnesses] and so forth—the minds to be remedied are not one.
Depending on many objects for discernment, each arises through its own specific activity.
Mental factors (*caitasika*) should not be conceptualized, for they arise in accordance with their corresponding objects.

They induce the threefold discrimination of the mind; their functions—such as experiencing the state, discerning characteristics, and engaging in activities like gain and loss—are termed the operations of attention (*manasikāra*) and so forth.
In the higher realms, fragrance and taste do not exist; The great elements and their derivatives are perceived accordingly.
Atoms have no intrinsic nature; The seven categories are not substantially real.
Subtle atoms combine without separation; Good and evil do not arise spontaneously.

The three characteristics do not exist apart from their conceptual designations; the twelve types of form within the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) should be known as non-associated. All these are merely provisionally established;
the nature of such provisional existence is sixfold, for each of those would entail two faults.
The three types of causes are not five; the characteristics of causes are briefly combined with their bonds.
Based on the distinctions of dependence and location, many kinds of establishments are formed.
Because the mind takes objects and so forth as its conditions, and because it is the object-condition for purification.
Due to four kinds of dissociation, eight unconditioned phenomena are established.
One should know that within the three realms there are twelve distinct aspects;
these consist of the objects to be countered and their counteragents, which function solely to suppress and subdue the seeds [of affliction].
The Dharma King, the salty taste of the ocean, long lifespans in the evil destinies, and multiple worlds sharing a single [time]: each has two kinds of causes and conditions.
The four afflictions associated with the mental consciousness are universal and arise simultaneously.
The indeterminate ceases at the very end; its nature follows that of whatever arises.
All successions of birth, as well as their manifestation and conditions, along with the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), objects, and coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*), each differ in twenty ways.
Because they arise in accordance with themselves, because they are seeds and entities,
because they give rise to four faults, and because of three causes of impurity;
there are thirteen distinctions between volition (*cetanā*) and what has been willed (*cetayitvā*).
Its fruits are sixfold and its stages three; karmic determination is of five kinds.
Self-action and so forth are fourfold, and those that ripen first are likewise four.
Furthermore, one should know there are nine types, which are simply two categories distinguished.
Death may be certain or uncertain; untimely death occurs due to six causes.
At the stage of clear comprehension, there are three types of minds; the intermediate state (antarābhava) may or may not exist.
Depending on other objects of perception, defiled minds arise.
Among the four types of birth, as well as within the three realms and five destinies, one should know that conventional truth consists of the meaning understood by the mind and its verbal expression;
its nature is the object of purification. Expedient means is called the ultimate truth.
One should know that these four types are subsumed under defilement and purification;
they are as yet unseen and unexperienced, like a disease and the cause for its cessation.
One should know that these Four Noble Truths each possess four characteristics and four aspects;
through the four types such as thorough knowledge (*parijñā*), there is a differentiation of cause and effect.
Their realization is free from contradiction; this is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and the same applies to their realization.
The three kinds of truths are exclusively wholesome; furthermore, two kinds should be known.
One should know that the seven bases have three kinds of supporting natures.
Skillfulness in those consists of two kinds, as extensively explained in the fourfold propositions and so forth.
The factors of dhyāna, their classification of obstacles, and their detailed establishment;
the distancing from suffering and agitation, and the progressive excellence of each subsequent factor.
The preparatory stages possess joy and agitation; only the first [dhyāna] can exhaust the outflows.
There are also two kinds of conditions for sound; by abandoning the eight attainments,
one dwells in happiness in the present life, is able to enter into clear realization,
and is praised as having liberation through perception— these four causes should be known.
One should know that the "taste of craving" and so forth consist of ten, six, and three types;
they are the signs of decline, the obstacles to the continuity [of the path], and their remedies, each with many further distinctions.
Those of sharp faculties and those who have undergone a change of birth should be known as having no falling back;
because they arise from a meditative absorption based on a lower stage and because they are born after having already abandoned desire.
Depending on the two vehicles or the Great Vehicle, [this occurs] by way of twenty-seven aspects.
One should know that right effort establishes the factors of enlightenment.
Through the three distinctions of body and so forth, one contemplates their reflected images;
by means of the three types of knowledge—such as that derived from hearing—one remains mindful of the Dharma without confusion.
One should know that there are nine types of what is to be remedied, two types of mental attention (*manasikāra*),
three distinctions in cultivation, and two types that are free from loss or destruction.
To sever dullness and agitation, there are two corresponding paths.
One observes the relinquishing of afflictions, And acts to exhaust the three types of craving.
To sever overweening pride, The perversions based on attachment to flavors,
And for the purpose of entering the three mental states, One cultivates the foundations of mindfulness.
Due to the distinctions of the faculties and so forth, the five *tanmātras* and the two [gross elements] are established;
one should know that the five [sense objects] are designated as such, and thus the three factors are brought to completion.
Having realized the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), non-arising occurs; there is no retrogression from the two causes and results.
Due to three causes, there is neither annihilation nor permanence; The three fruits are predicted by means of the three causes.
All virtues are established Through seventeen types of supremacy;
Their distinctions are boundless, Because they remedy the obstacles to be overcome.
Contemplating the meaning, pleasure, and suffering; Attention, and abiding;
difficulty and characteristics; The extraordinary and the non-extraordinary;
Lineage, the Tathāgata’s teaching, Many Buddhas, and the two vehicles.
The fivefold and tenfold [categories], the six and sixfold principles,
the wondrous powers of the Buddhas, their pure resultant lands,
liberation, and the Dharma-body— these are equal, inconceivable, and unsurpassed.
Although it does not employ preparatory effort, it is induced by the power of prior vows;
arising in dependence on the unconditioned, its activity is without dual characteristics.
It proclaims all phenomena and the distinct analysis of the Prātimokṣa.
The eleven characteristics of all phenomena are the fundamental treasury of this Sūtra and Vinaya.
These characteristics, their cessation, the skillful means for non-destruction,
those two fruits, and their distinctions— these are the summarized meaning of all the Sūtras.
A brief explanation of the path of yoga: Based on the sublime Dharma as it has been heard, Through śamatha and vipaśyanā, One achieves accomplishment by means of the image.
—From the *Śāsanodbhāvana-kārikā* (Verses for Proclaiming the Holy Teaching).
